summary.en: The Byrds open the folk-rock wave; its source is Bob Dylan.
summary.zh: The Byrds拉开了民谣摇滚潮流的序幕，而这股潮流的源头正是Bob Dylan。

body.zh:
The Byrds拉开了民谣摇滚潮流的序幕，而这股潮流的源头正是Bob Dylan。

1960年代中期，Bob Dylan是美国的回应潮流里的重要人物。但在那段由英国艺人统治榜单的日子里，Dylan当然并非唯一推动局面改变的人。关于Bob Dylan，我们常会听到65年夏天的Newport Folk音乐节、《Like a Rolling Stone》等一系列故事。此外，我们必须再谈谈The Byrds的音乐，因为在很多方面，它与Bob Dylan有非常紧密的联系。

The Byrds由吉他手Roger McGuinn发起，David Crosby、Gene Clark、Chris Hillman和Micheal Clarke随后加入。和许多音乐人一样，McGuinn-Crosby这个二人组也是从格林威治村的民谣音乐圈子开始打出名堂的。但自那时起，一场面向西海岸的迁移开始在音乐产业内部成形。其实在整个60年代里，你都能明显看出，这个国家的音乐产业在很大程度上从纽约转移到了洛杉矶。洛杉矶具备许多天然的优势。其中之一是，电视和电影产业的重心就在那里。因此，那里有许多熟悉制作技术的老手，也有许多设备不错的录音棚等等。于是McGuinn想办法来到了洛杉矶，开始发展他的民谣音乐事业；唱一些传统的民谣，也唱一些Beatles的歌——用的是民谣的演奏方式，这在当时看来是有点奇怪的。但你已经可以看出来，McGuinn想要追随的是Beatles的方向。The byrds最初的名字叫the Beefeaters。乐队有一首叫《Mr. Tambourine Man》的歌，它其实是Dylan的手笔。但Dylan至此还没亲自录过这首歌。他稍后做了这件事，Ramblin' Jack Elliott也参加了录音工作。由于演奏过程中有乐器跑调了，他们决定弃用这份录音。而当时the Byrds的制作人Terry Melcher拿到了它，the Byrds听说了这件事，于是就此开始炮制另一个版本的《Mr. Tambourine Man》。他们一开始用了十二弦民谣吉他伴奏，这与60年代上半叶的民谣复兴风格十分相似，比如说New Christie Minstrels这类组合。但随后在1965年的夏天，《A Hard Day’s Night》上映了。The Byrds的成员也去看了这部电影。最初他们和其他人一样，被Beatles和Beatles热潮迷得神魂颠倒——这太棒了，这就是我们想做的事情，我们想变得和他们一样。但the Byrds注意到，George Harrison在电影里弹奏了一把Rickenbacker十二弦吉他。当时McGuinn已经在弹奏一把十二弦民谣吉他，而电影里这把Rickenbacker十二弦电吉他只有六个琴栓，从正面来看它和普通吉他无异，但如果把它转个角度，你就会发现它还有另外六个琴栓用于调整六根琴弦，如此总计十二个琴栓。Roger McGuinn觉得George Harrison弹奏这把吉他的样子太棒了，这就是他想做的事情，他要买一把这样的吉他。事实上，Rickenbacker吉他的产地正是南加州。他可以直接走进一家琴行，用一把十二弦民谣吉他、一把班卓琴或类似的东西来交换一把崭新的Rickenbacker吉他。他们决定用这把Rickenbacker十二弦电吉他来录制自家版本的《Mr. Tambourine Man》。那种叮叮当当的民谣摇滚声响，就此成为了流行音乐产业的一个标志。想想REM和Tom Petty这样的乐队，他们都在运用这种叮叮当当的声响。一切都源于1965年的那一刻，Roger McGuinn拿起了《Hard Day’s Night》中的同款吉他，用它来演奏Bob Dylan的歌曲。就是这样。他还说，自己弹的前奏受到了巴赫《Jesu Joy Of Man’s Desiring》的影响。当这些元素结合在一起时，冠军单曲《Mr. Tambourine Man》便诞生了。它在1965年4月发行，正好与《Like A Rolling Stone》在榜单上碰面。有趣的是，包括《Mr. Tambourine Man》在内的这两首Bob Dylan歌曲，一首由Dylan创作但不由他自己演绎，另一首同样由他创作同时又由他演绎。这可以说是代表了他当时的事业的两个侧面。《Mr. Tambourine Man》中的有趣元素，不止于Beatles风格的吉他碰上了Dylan的歌曲以及受到巴赫影响的前奏；它还是由 Phil Spector曾合作过的录音棚乐队进行伴奏的。实际上他们也曾在《Don’t Worry Baby》这首单曲中与The Beach Boys合作。在录制《Mr. Tambourine Man》时，这些录音棚乐手们回忆起了那段经历；然后，Terry Melcher提议加入一些The Beach Boys的感觉。于是他们把《Don’t Worry Baby》里的Beach Boys风格融入到了McGuinn的演奏之中。 如此就有了《Mr. Tambourine Man》。

你应该有留意到，我刚刚提及了一支录音棚乐队。其实，Roger McGuinn是乐队里唯一参与了《Mr. Tambourine Man》的配乐演奏的成员，余下的工作全是由录音棚乐队完成的。其他the Byrds成员只是参与了演唱。几年后The Monkees的作品面世，而谈及他们时，我们会讲到The Monkees的成员有多么不真实、甚至不在自己的唱片中演奏。但实际上，在《Mr. Tambourine Man》这首无疑具有真实性的民谣摇滚经典中，大部分的演奏也是由录音棚乐队完成的。不过在此之后，the Byrds的成员开始自己负责歌曲中的演奏，并推出了《All I Really Want to Do》这首热门单曲。这其中有一件关于Cher的趣事，我回头会提到它。《Turn, Turn, Turn》，一首出自Pete Seeger的歌曲，（被the Byrds翻唱后）也在1965年秋天登上了冠军宝座。而《Eight Miles High》这首歌，McGuinn说它讲的是一架在7英里高空飞行的跨国航班，但“7英里”放在歌词里听着不合韵律，于是就改成了8英里。但当然了，每个人都认为这些歌词讲的是毒品。因此这首歌只在1966年春天拿到了第14名的最高排位，最终还因为它与毒品有关的说法在电台间流传而被撤下榜单。这首歌也受到了John Coltrane的深刻影响，开头那段用十二弦弹奏的吉他乐句，在我看来，就直接引用自John Coltrane的歌曲《India》。这就是the Byrds的经历，将Dylan风格的民谣歌曲，与那种叮叮当当的声响融合起来。说到我之前提过的这种叮叮当当的声响，制作人Tom Wilson将是其重要人物之一，是这一讨论中的重要组成部分。

让我们来聊聊Simon and Garfunkel及其大获成功的经过。这是又一个出身纽约的重要组合，其实他们也一直留在纽约发展。Simon and Garfunkel在50年代以兄弟组合Tom and Jerry的名号出道，有一支叫做《Hey Schoolgirl》的单曲，还算流行。他们甚至作为青少年版的Everly Brothers登上了电视节目American bandstand。但随后他们从学校毕业，去做了一些别的事情；后来又以Simon and Garfunkel的名号、作为民谣复兴运动的一份子回到大众视野之中，并于1964年发行了一张全原声专辑《Wednesday Morning, 3 A.M.》。专辑并未取得成功。其中有一首歌叫《The Sound of Silence》，但它还不是大家耳熟能详的那个版本。总之，这张专辑反响不佳。Paul Simon去英格兰继续唱歌了，而Art Garfunkel，我想，是去读了个研究生之类的。当时他们并未以Simon and Garfunkel的名义继续活动。但到了1965年夏天，《Mr. Tambourine Man》登上榜单、Dylan的歌曲也开始走红，制作人Tom Wilson就想起了与Dylan同属Columbia唱片公司的专辑《Wednesday Morning, 3 A.M.》。他背着Paul Simon和Art Garfunkel，将一批乐手带进录音棚，调取了《The Sound of Silence》的原版录音，往里头加入了电吉他、贝斯和鼓。那么，你要如何往已录制完成的歌曲中添加东西呢？要是听过录音，这就很容易说清楚了。歌曲的头几个小节保留了只有民谣吉他伴奏的配置，这样一来，乐手就不难跟上节奏了。几个小节后，电吉他切入，贝斯和鼓也随之切入。所以，在原唱毫不知情的前提下，这首歌在美国重新发行，并在1965年夺得了榜单冠军。想象一下Paul Simon接到电话的情景吧： “听着，Paul，这里是你的唱片公司。你猜怎么着？你有首歌在美国红了！” “我的歌在美国红了，这是什么意思？”这就是事情的来龙去脉。Tom Wilson所做的事情 ，不过是往一首原声民谣歌曲里加入了电吉他、贝斯和鼓；而，真的，这就是民谣摇滚的定义。Simon and Garfunkel接着录制了《The Sound of Silence》这张专辑，这大概就是你们熟知的版本了。其他的一些歌曲，比如1966年的《Homeward Bound》和《I Am a Rock》，更令他们成为了那个时代最重要的艺人之一。

同样在洛杉矶打出名堂的，还有The Mamas & The Papas。他们最初也在纽约成军，也和the Byrds一样转战到了洛杉矶。他们是民谣摇滚风潮中的晚辈。这支乐队由John Philips领衔，队内有两名男性和两名女性，也就是所谓的爸爸 (The Papas) 和妈妈 (The Mamas)，包括被称作Cass妈妈的Cass Elliot，很大程度上她是乐队里的明星人物。不过，大部分的歌曲写作、和声与器乐编排，都由John Phillips负责。他们的第一支大热单曲《California Dreamin’》，在1966年拿下了第4名。他们的冠军单曲则诞生于1966年，叫做《Monday, Monday》。此时，民谣摇滚乐队圈中发生了另一件事。由于the Byrds在翻唱Dylan的歌曲后获得了空前成功，其他乐队或是同样去找Dylan的歌来翻唱，或是尝试在创作中模仿Dylan的手法。有个叫做Barry McGuire的人，其单曲在1965年秋天夺得了冠军。当时距离民谣摇滚出现、也即《Mr. Tambourine Man》发行只过去了数月。那首歌叫做《Eve of Destruction》。歌曲的作者P.F. Solan最初是接到了Lou Adler与唱片公司分配的任务，得去写一首并非出自Dylan、但听起来就像是Dylan的歌曲。于是，他创作了《Eve of Destruction》，Barry McGuire也由此有了一首冠军单曲。The Turtles，另外一支来自洛杉矶的乐队，翻唱了Dylan的《It Ain’t Me Babe》，并凭借这首翻唱曲目在1965年拿到了榜单第8名。 The Turtles由Mark Volman和Howard Kaylan这两名歌手领军，后来改名为Phlorescent Leech and Eddie或称Flo and Eddie——这时他们开始现身于Frank Zappa的专辑，并在70年代开启了单飞生涯。但早些时候，他们仍是the Turtles乐队。《It Ain’t Me Babe》是一首很棒的单曲。而他们的《Happy Together》，于不久后的1967年面世的冠军单曲，更是1960年代的代表性美国流行单曲之一。

那么，关于民谣摇滚的讨论就差不多到这里了。但在1960年代的美国的回应中，还有其他元素可供探讨。到了下节课，我们将转头介绍Phil Spector的光辉遗产。
body.en:
The Byrds open the folk-rock wave; its source is Bob Dylan.

In the mid-1960s Dylan is a central figure in America’s reply. But while British acts rule the charts, he is not the only one shifting the ground. We hear Newport summer 1965, “Like a Rolling Stone,” and related stories. We also need the Byrds—tightly tied to Dylan in many ways.

The Byrds start with guitarist Roger McGuinn; David Crosby, Gene Clark, Chris Hillman, and Michael Clarke join. Like many, the McGuinn–Crosby pair first make a name in the Greenwich Village folk circle. Then a westward migration takes shape inside the industry. Across the 1960s you can see the business move largely from New York to Los Angeles. L.A. has natural advantages—one is TV and film centered there—so skilled production hands and decent studios are plentiful. McGuinn works his way west, building a folk career: traditional folk plus Beatles songs played as folk—odd then, but you already see him aiming Beatle-ward. Early name: the Beefeaters. They have “Mr. Tambourine Man,” written by Dylan, who has not yet recorded his own cut. He does later; Ramblin’ Jack Elliott is on that session. An out-of-tune instrument leads them to scrap it. Producer Terry Melcher gets the song; the Byrds hear of it and start their version. First they use twelve-string acoustic folk guitar, close to early-1960s revival acts like the New Christy Minstrels. Then summer 1965: A Hard Day’s Night opens. The Byrds see it. At first they are as Beatle-mad as anyone—that is what they want to be. But they notice George Harrison’s Rickenbacker twelve-string electric: six pegs facing you like a normal guitar, six more at an angle for the second set of strings. McGuinn already plays twelve-string acoustic; he wants that Rickenbacker. Rickenbacker is made in Southern California—he can walk into a shop and trade a twelve-string acoustic, a banjo, or similar for a new one. They record “Mr. Tambourine Man” on that Rickenbacker twelve-string electric. That jangly folk-rock sound becomes a pop-industry signature. Think R.E.M. and Tom Petty—jangly sound tracing to that 1965 moment when McGuinn takes the Hard Day’s Night guitar and plays a Dylan song. He also says the intro is shaped by Bach’s “Jesu, Joy of Man’s Desiring.” Combined, the No. 1 single “Mr. Tambourine Man” appears—issued April 1965, meeting “Like a Rolling Stone” on the charts. Two Dylan songs: one written but not sung by him; one written and sung by him—two sides of his career then. Interesting elements beyond Beatles-style guitar on a Dylan song and a Bach-tinged intro: session players who had worked with Phil Spector—and with the Beach Boys on “Don’t Worry Baby”—back the track. Melcher asks for some Beach Boys feel; they fold that “Don’t Worry Baby” approach into McGuinn’s playing. That is “Mr. Tambourine Man.”

Note: I mentioned a session band. McGuinn is the only Byrd who plays on the instrumental track; the rest is studio players. Other Byrds only sing. Years later we will say the Monkees do not even play on their records—but on this authentic folk-rock classic, most of the playing is also session work. Afterward the Byrds play their own instruments and cut the hit “All I Really Want to Do”—a Cher story I will return to. “Turn! Turn! Turn!” (from Pete Seeger) also hits No. 1 in fall 1965. “Eight Miles High”: McGuinn says it is about a transatlantic flight at seven miles; “seven” does not scan, so eight. Everyone hears drugs anyway. It peaks at No. 14 in spring 1966 and is pulled from radio as a drug song. It is also deeply shaped by John Coltrane; the opening twelve-string line, to my ear, quotes Coltrane’s “India.” That is the Byrds path: Dylan-style folk songs plus that jangle. Tom Wilson will also matter for this jangle discussion.

Simon and Garfunkel’s breakthrough: another important New York act that stays in New York. In the 1950s they are the teen duo Tom and Jerry—“Hey Schoolgirl,” even American Bandstand as a teen Everly Brothers. After school they go other ways, then return as Simon and Garfunkel in the folk revival with the all-acoustic Wednesday Morning, 3 A.M. (1964)—no success. It includes “The Sound of Silence,” not yet the famous version. Paul Simon goes to England to sing; Art Garfunkel, I think, goes to graduate school. They are not active as Simon and Garfunkel. Summer 1965: “Mr. Tambourine Man” charts, Dylan songs rise; producer Tom Wilson recalls the Columbia LP Wednesday Morning, 3 A.M. Behind Simon and Garfunkel’s backs he brings players in, pulls the original “Sound of Silence,” and adds electric guitar, bass, and drums. How do you overdub a finished track? Listen and it is clear: the first bars stay folk-guitar only so players can lock the groove; then electric guitar, bass, and drums enter. The song is reissued in the U.S. without the artists knowing and hits No. 1 in 1965. Imagine Paul Simon’s phone call: “Paul, your label—your song is a hit in America.” “What does that mean?” That is the story. Wilson simply adds electric guitar, bass, and drums to an acoustic folk song—really the definition of folk rock. They then record the Sound of Silence album—the version most people know. Songs like 1966’s “Homeward Bound” and “I Am a Rock” help make them among the era’s key acts.

Also rising in L.A.: the Mamas & the Papas. Formed in New York, they move west like the Byrds—later arrivals in the folk-rock wave. Led by John Phillips: two men, two women—the Papas and Mamas, including Cass Elliot (“Mama Cass”), largely the star presence. Most writing, harmony, and arranging is John Phillips. First big single “California Dreamin’” reaches No. 4 in 1966; the No. 1 is 1966’s “Monday, Monday.” Another folk-rock beat: after the Byrds’ Dylan covers explode, others cover Dylan or imitate his writing. Barry McGuire hits No. 1 in fall 1965—only months after “Mr. Tambourine Man”—with “Eve of Destruction,” written by P. F. Sloan on assignment from Lou Adler and the label to write something that is not Dylan but sounds like Dylan. The Turtles, another L.A. band, cover Dylan’s “It Ain’t Me Babe” and reach No. 8 in 1965. Fronted by Mark Volman and Howard Kaylan, later Phlorescent Leech and Eddie / Flo & Eddie—Frank Zappa albums, then 1970s solo work—but earlier they are the Turtles. “It Ain’t Me Babe” is a fine single; their 1967 No. 1 “Happy Together” is one of the decade’s representative American pop singles.

That is enough on folk rock for now. America’s reply has other strands. Next: Phil Spector’s lasting legacy.
